messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan’s hands, which could meticulously bone a fish or plate a delicate sauce, would often tremble for no reason he could name. At forty-four, he had built a life around the controlled chaos of a professional kitchen, a world of heat, noise, and precision that felt a universe away from the one he had fled. The trauma had happened twelve years ago, but it lived in the tense set of his shoulders and the way his eyes darted to any sudden movement. It was the memory of a marketplace, the smell of spices and dust, the bright midday sun glinting off the stalls. He had been buying vegetables when the world dissolved into a concussive roar. The memory itself was a stubborn fog; he could recall the moments before, the vibrant colours, but the event itself was a silent film of disjointed images he couldn't seem to put into words. Sometimes, when he tried to force the narrative, a profound numbness would descend, as if he were watching a stranger’s tragedy. At other times, a wave of grief so total it threatened to drown him would rise up, leaving him breathless with the weight of who was lost.

This fractured recall was the foundation for a brutal self-assessment. The gaps in his memory were not a mercy but a source of profound guilt. He was certain that in those missing seconds, he had failed. The thought, a searing constant, was that he should have done more, that he had frozen when others needed him. This belief that he was unforgivably culpable was cemented by the sheer fact of his own survival. This guilt made him exquisitely sensitive to any reminder of the event. The distant wail of an ambulance was no longer just a sound; it was an echo of the aftermath, a signal that sent a jolt of panic through him. The sight of a police officer’s uniform on his commute would cause his focus to narrow, his body bracing for an impact that never came.

These moments of being triggered would instantly activate a sense of pervasive threat. His mind, which needed to track a dozen orders at once in the kitchen, would shatter into a million useless pieces, making it impossible to concentrate. He began to live in a state of high alert, his senses perpetually scanning for danger. Before entering any room, even the familiar staff breakroom, he would instinctively locate all the exits, a mental map of escape routes forming before he could even register the faces of his colleagues. On days when this feeling of imminent danger was particularly acute, the fragmented images of the marketplace would surface unbidden, as if his mind were forced to review the evidence of the threat he was trying so hard to preempt. This constant state of vigilance only made his triggers more potent; being on guard meant he was the first to notice the flashing lights of a passing emergency vehicle, a sight that would send him right back into the panicked alertness he was trying to escape.

This constant feeling of being unsafe dictated his behaviour. He started taking longer, more convoluted routes to work, purely to avoid walking through a large, open plaza that left him feeling exposed and vulnerable. This carefully curated detour became its own kind of reminder; the extra ten minutes he spent walking each morning were a silent, daily testament to the event, ensuring it was never far from his mind and making him even more sensitive to other cues, like a passing police car. His belief that he was permanently damaged, that some essential part of his courage had been destroyed in the blast, made this avoidance feel not like a choice, but a necessity. This certainty that he was broken meant he walked through the world already defeated, interpreting neutral situations as latently dangerous because he felt he no longer had the resources to cope. The feeling of threat would become so overwhelming that he would seek escape, and avoiding open spaces or the sight of uniforms became his primary strategy. When a new line cook badly cut his hand one evening, the sight of the wound and the ensuing talk of the accident sent Rohan into a tailspin. He felt the walls of the kitchen closing in. Trapped and panicked, he found himself nodding mutely at every frantic instruction from the sous chef, his voice gone, becoming overly compliant and small in a desperate, unconscious bid not to be noticed, not to be a target.

These strategies, meant to keep him safe, instead became the bars of his cage. Every time he altered his route to avoid the plaza, it reinforced the core belief that he was broken and the world was a dangerous place. This constant avoidance also starved his memory of any new, corrective information, leaving the trauma to exist in its raw, unprocessed state, a loop of silent images and searing guilt. The act of constantly scanning for exits and uniforms kept his nervous system buzzing with threat, which in turn made it even harder to concentrate, further convincing him he was failing. The cycle had tightened over the years, shrinking his world until it was little more than his small apartment and the kitchen. It was after the incident with the injured cook, when his boss gently commented on his distraction, that Rohan realised he was at risk of losing the one thing that gave him structure. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a terrifying question: what if the damage truly was permanent, and this half-life of fear was all that was left for him?
